records.rationale: Correct definition and invariant row space/rank. Row operations need not preserve the column space or determinant, as the answer explains.

evidence.finding: Elementary row operations are multiplication on the left by invertible matrices. They preserve row span and rank; they can transform the column span and change determinant by a known factor.
Left multiplication by invertible E gives row(EA)=row(A) and rank(EA)=rank(A). A=[[1,0],[0,0]] and its row-swapped matrix have distinct column spans.

'Generally different' means not invariant, not that every row operation changes those quantities. Full-rank square matrices all have the full ambient column space; operations other than type 3 can also leave a determinant unchanged.

evidence.title: Ito, Xiang and Zou, An Inexact Uzawa Algorithm for Generalized Saddle-Point Problems
evidence.finding: Uzawa-type algorithms and robustness depend on block assumptions, parameters and preconditioning; variants cover symmetric and nonsymmetric saddle-point systems.

evidence.title: Nataf and Tournier, A GenEO Domain Decomposition method for Saddle Point problems
evidence.finding: Section 1 describes direct solvers for suitably sized saddle-point problems as robust with predictable efficiency, with memory requirements limiting large problems. Iterative and preconditioned alternatives address that scaling.

For A positive definite and full-row-rank B, eliminating the primal variable gives the multiplier Schur complement B*A^-1*B^T. Uzawa acts iteratively on that multiplier equation, while a full indefinite factorization solves the coupled block system.

This comparison assumes a nonsingular well-posed saddle problem and the standard SPD-primal-block Uzawa setting. Direct-solver memory, conditioning and pivoting still matter; generalized Uzawa variants have other assumptions.
